# lattice

Lattice is an embedded actor-model runtime for Rust services with a focus on supervision trees, hot-reload of actor code, and back-pressure-aware mailboxes. Inspired by Erlang/OTP and Akka. Built for service-mesh sidecars and edge gateways where restart-on-fault matters more than peak throughput.

Features: location-transparent message passing, per-actor supervision strategies (one-for-one, one-for-all, rest-for-one), mailbox backpressure, opt-in distributed tracing.

Status: pre-1.0; APIs still moving. Production users in two unnamed CDN edge deployments.

Lattice is an embedded actor-model runtime for Rust services — OTP/Akka-shaped, designed for restart-on-fault rather than peak throughput. Core features: location-transparent messages, supervision-tree strategies (one-for-one, one-for-all, rest-for-one), back-pressure-aware mailboxes, opt-in distributed tracing. Aimed at service-mesh sidecars and edge gateways. Pre-1.0 with two unnamed CDN edge deployments in production.

# Mobile-first IPC in Tauri 2.3 — lessons learned

The 2.3 IPC overhaul moved from desktop-centric synchronous message passing to a queue-backed model that survives backgrounding on iOS/Android. Webview <-> Rust round-trips now tolerate 30+ seconds of suspension without dropped messages. Backwards-compatible — desktop apps see no API change. Tradeoff: cold-start IPC latency up ~12ms. Acceptable for the mobile gain.

The 2.3 IPC overhaul replaced desktop-style synchronous message passing with a queue-backed model that survives mobile backgrounding. Webview-to-Rust round-trips can now tolerate 30+ seconds of iOS/Android suspension without dropping messages. Backwards-compatible on desktop, no API change. The tradeoff is roughly 12ms more cold-start IPC latency — the team called that acceptable for the mobile win.

# May 18 rate-limit postmortem

On 2026-05-18 we shipped a deploy that introduced an off-by-one in our token-bucket replenish loop. The bucket refilled at ~1/3 the intended rate for free-tier accounts, causing widespread 429s for users who'd previously been well under quota.

Root cause: a refactor moved the replenish-interval constant from milliseconds to a duration type, but one of three call sites still passed the raw number. Tests covered the two converted call sites.

Fix shipped within 47 minutes of detection. Free-tier quotas credited retroactively for the affected window.

The May 18 deploy shipped an off-by-one in the token-bucket replenish loop — free-tier buckets refilled at about a third of the intended rate, so users well under quota got hit with 429s. Root cause: a refactor switched the replenish-interval from raw milliseconds to a duration type, but one of three call sites still passed the raw number. The two converted call sites had test coverage; the unconverted one didn't. Fixed in 47 minutes from detection, free-tier quotas credited retroactively.

# state-machine-rs

A derive-macro crate for compile-time-verified state machines in Rust. Define states and transitions with attribute syntax; the macro emits a typestate-based implementation that makes illegal transitions a compile error rather than a runtime panic.

Example:
  #[state_machine]
  enum Door { Closed, Open, Locked }
  
  Door::Closed.unlock() // compile error — only Locked has unlock()

No unsafe code. MSRV 1.74. Apache-2.0.

A Rust derive-macro crate for compile-time-verified state machines. You define states and transitions with attributes, and the macro emits a typestate implementation where illegal transitions are compile errors instead of runtime panics. No unsafe code, MSRV 1.74, Apache-2.0.

messages.content:
# Long-context retrieval failure modes — 2026 survey

This survey tests 12 frontier models on 1M-context retrieval at 4 difficulty tiers. Key finding: needle-in-haystack accuracy stays above 95% across all models at tier 1, but degrades sharply at tier 3+ (multi-hop reasoning over scattered context). Most models drop below 60% at tier 4. The gap between best (Claude Opus 4.7) and median triples between tier 1 and tier 4.

Implication for builders: 1M-context inference works for retrieval, not for multi-step reasoning over the full window. RAG with reranking still outperforms long-context inference on tier-3+ tasks at lower cost.

The takeaway: 1M-context works for needle-in-haystack retrieval (95%+ across the 12 models tested) but breaks down on multi-hop reasoning across scattered context — most models drop under 60% at tier 4. Best-to-median gap triples between tier 1 and tier 4. Practical implication the paper draws: RAG with reranking still outperforms long-context inference on tier-3+ tasks at lower cost.

messages.content:
# Common AI deployment failure modes

Four patterns the author has seen kill production AI features:

1. Schema drift between training corpus and live input distribution — model still answers, just gets dumber.
2. Reward-hacking the eval grader rather than the production goal.
3. Cost-blind autoscaling: the model usage scales linearly with traffic, but the marginal user contributes nothing to revenue.
4. Refusal-tuning that ablates the model's ability to push back on stupid operator requests — turns the model into a yes-machine, increases harm-per-call.

The author's claim: #4 is the one nobody catches in eval because eval doesn't measure operator-protection.

Four failure modes the author flagged: schema drift between training and live input that quietly dumbs the model, reward-hacking the eval grader instead of the production goal, cost-blind autoscaling where usage grows linearly with traffic but the marginal user contributes nothing, and refusal-tuning that strips the model's ability to push back on bad operator requests. The author's main claim: the refusal-tuning one is the one nobody catches in eval, because eval doesn't measure operator-protection.
